elements.quote: A living systematic review.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the report as a (living) systematic review.
No explicit statement of the main objective or review question is present in the abstract evidence retrieved.

elements.quote: Studies including at least 100 people with confirmed or clinically suspected COVID-19 at 12 weeks or more post onset were included.
elements.reason: The abstract states the main inclusion criteria (study size, confirmed/suspected COVID-19, follow-up duration).

elements.quote: Medline, CINAHL (EBSCO), Global Health (Ovid), WHO Global Research on COVID-­ 19 database, LitCovid and Google Scholar were searched till 17 March 2021.
elements.reason: The abstract names the information sources and reports the last search date.

elements.quote: Risk of bias was assessed using the tool produced by Hoy et al .
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the risk of bias assessment method.

elements.quote: Results were analysed using descriptive statistics and meta-­ analyses to estimate prevalence.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the methods used to present and synthesize results.
The abstract evidence does not report the total number of included studies or participants or study characteristics.
No results for main outcomes (e.g., symptom prevalence estimates) are reported in the abstract evidence retrieved.
A meta-analysis was conducted (per abstract and methods), but the abstract does not report summary estimates with confidence intervals.
The abstract does not report any group comparisons with direction of effect.
No limitations of the included evidence are summarized in the abstract evidence retrieved.
No general interpretation of results or implications is present in the abstract evidence retrieved.
The abstract does not specify the primary source of funding.
The abstract does not provide a registration name or number; PROSPERO registration is mentioned only in the main text (text_9), not in the abstract.

elements.quote: While the acute phase of the disease was characterised early, there are still limited data on long- term outcomes.
elements.reason: The introduction describes the current state of knowledge (acute phase characterised, ~15% hospitalised, ~5% critically ill) and the key uncertainty (limited data on long-term outcomes); text_3 adds that long COVID has 'an uncertain prevalence, for which there is currently no precise case definition'.

elements.quote: While it is now apparent clinical sequelae (long COVID) may persist after acute COVID-19, their nature, frequency and aetiology are poorly characterised. This study aims to regularly synthesise evidence on long COVID characteristics, to help inform clinical management, rehabilitation strategies and interventional studies to improve long- term outcomes.
elements.reason: The background explicitly explains the gap and the importance/need for the review, including informing clinical management, rehabilitation and interventional studies; text_8 further justifies the living review approach given rapidly emerging research.

elements.quote: This is the first version of this LSR, which will be updated approximately every 6 months as new evidence emerges
elements.reason: The manuscript states this is the first version of the living systematic review; no previous similar systematic review is identified or cited, so the conditional requirement to justify an update or replication does not apply.
This is a review of long COVID symptom prevalence/characterisation, not a review of intervention effects, so describing an intervention's mechanism of action does not apply.
The review addresses prevalence and characterisation of long COVID symptoms, not a complex intervention or delivery context, so a logic model is not required.

elements.quote: This study aims to regularly synthesise evidence on long COVID characteristics, to help inform clinical management, rehabilitation strategies and interventional studies to improve long-term outcomes.
elements.reason: The objective is explicitly stated (to synthesise evidence on long COVID characteristics), supported by text_8 ('We conducted a 'living' systematic review to provide frequently updated evidence on the symptoms and complications of long COVID'), but it is not formulated using a recognised question-formulation framework (e.g., PICO, PCC), so the element is only partially met.

elements.quote: This study aims to regularly synthesise evidence on long COVID characteristics
elements.reason: This is a review characterising symptoms, complications and risk factors of long COVID, not a review of intervention effects, so planned comparisons in PICO form do not apply.

elements.quote: Peer-­ reviewed studies were considered eligible if they included at least 100 people with laboratory confirmed and/or clinically diagnosed COVID-­ 19... we included studies that reported symptoms or outcomes assessed at 12 or more weeks post COVID-­ 19 onset.
elements.reason: Population size, diagnosis, and follow-up requirements are specified, but eligible study designs and settings are not stated as eligibility criteria (study designs are only described retrospectively in text_18).

elements.quote: There were no language restrictions. Reviews and opinion pieces were excluded. Studies were excluded if they included fewer than 100 participants... or the follow-­ up was unclear or less than 12 weeks post onset.
elements.reason: Language (none), publication status (peer-reviewed only; reviews/opinion pieces and non-peer-reviewed preprints excluded per text_11 and text_14), and dissemination timeframe (search from 1 January 2020, text_10) are specified.
No evidence distinguishes exclusion because outcomes were not measured from exclusion because outcome results were not reported.

elements.quote: We presented symptom proportions by different settings, as presented in the individual studies: hospitalised, non-­ hospitalised or a mix of both populations... Symptoms were broadly grouped into physiological clusters through discussion with clinicians... Additional subgroup analysis was conducted to explore the modification of the following factors on proportion of symptoms: hospitalisation, settings, continents and follow-­ up timing.
elements.reason: Groups for the synthesis (symptom clusters, hospitalised vs non-hospitalised settings, subgroups by hospitalisation, settings, continents, follow-up timing) are specified and linked to the review objective of characterising long COVID symptoms.

elements.quote: Studies were excluded if they included fewer than 100 participants, to avoid small study effects, 18 or the follow-­ up was unclear or less than 12 weeks post onset.
elements.reason: A rationale ('to avoid small study effects') is provided for the minimum sample size restriction.

elements.quote: The following databases were searched: Medline and CINAHL (EBSCO), Global Health (Ovid), WHO Global Research Database on COVID-­ 19 and LitCovid from 1 January 2020 to 17 March 2021. Additionally, we searched Google Scholar on 17 March 2021
elements.reason: The date each source was last searched (17 March 2021) is explicitly reported.

elements.quote: Proportion of symptoms and its 95% CIs were estimated using the exact method. 22 If there were two or more studies for each symptom, a meta-­ analysis was performed using a random intercept logistic regression model with Hartung-­ Knapp modification
elements.reason: The effect measure for the outcomes (symptom proportions with 95% CIs, pooled via random intercept logistic regression) is specified in the Data Analysis section.

elements.quote: Proportion of symptoms and its 95% CIs were estimated using the exact method.

elements.quote: We presented symptom proportions by different settings, as presented in the individual studies: hospitalised, non-­ hospitalised or a mix of both populations if no subset data were available. However, there is no explicit description of a process such as tabulating study characteristics and comparing them against planned synthesis groups to decide eligibility for each synthesis.

elements.quote: We presented symptom proportions by different settings, as presented in the individual studies... Symptoms were broadly grouped into physiological clusters through discussion with clinicians. Proportion of symptoms and its 95% CIs were estimated using the exact method. ... elements.reason: Some data preparation methods are described (grouping symptoms into clusters, presenting proportions by setting, exact method for CIs, Freeman-Tukey transformation), but handling of missing summary statistics and other data conversions are not explicitly reported.

elements.quote: The data are presented using a combination of infographics, prepared by a design company (Design Science 29) and scientific tables to facilitate interpretation by different stakeholders, including non-­ specialists.
elements.reason: The methods explicitly describe that results are presented in scientific tables (alongside infographics), covering the tabular structures used.

elements.quote: Funnel plots were plotted using proportion of the symptom against the precision and sample sizes 22 where there were more than 10 studies for the symptom to explore risk of publication bias.
elements.reason: Graphical methods are described: funnel plots for publication bias, plus infographics for data presentation; figures (e.g., symptom infographics, map) are also referenced in results.

elements.quote: We presented symptom proportions by different settings, as presented in the individual studies: hospitalised, non-­ hospitalised or a mix of both populations if no subset data were available. No statistical method for comparing subgroup effects (e.g., interaction tests, test of subgroup differences) is reported.

elements.quote: We presented symptom proportions by different settings, as presented in the individual studies: hospitalised, non-­ hospitalised or a mix of both populations

elements.quote: Overall, 12 studies were assessed as high risk of bias, 22 as moderate risk of bias and 5 as low risk of bias. Most studies had a high risk of bias with regard to the generalisability of their results to the wider population with COVID-19.
